source_text: Καὶ τάχα οὐκ ἐλάττων ὁ κίνδυνος τῷ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ θεοῦ ἢ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἐφ᾿ ἃ μὴ χρὴ κατάγοντι, ἤπερ τῷ τὰ κατά τινα ἀπόῤῥητον λόγον ὀνόματα ἐναλλάσσοντι καὶ τὰ μὲν κατὰ τῶν ἐλαττόνων φέροντι ἐπὶ τὰ κρείττονα τὰ δὲ κατὰ τῶν κρειττόνων ἐπὶ τὰ ἥττονα. καὶ οὐ λέγω ὅτι τῷ Διῒ εὐθέως συνεξακούεται ὁ Κρόνου καὶ Ῥέας υἱὸς καὶ Ἥρας ἀνὴρ καὶ Ποσειδῶνος ἀδελφὸς καὶ Ἀθηνᾶς καὶ Ἀρτέμιδος πατὴρ καὶ ὁ τῇ θυγατρὶ Περσεφόνῃ μιγεὶς, ἢ τῷ Ἀπόλλωνι συνεξακούεται ὁ Λητοῦς καὶ Διὸς υἱὸς καὶ Ἀρτέμιδος ἀδελφὸς καὶ Ἑρμοῦ ὁμοπάτριος ἀδελφὸς, καὶ ὅσα ἄλλα φέρουσιν οἱ σοφοὶ Κέλσου τῶν δογμάτων πατέρες καὶ ἀρχαῖοι θεολόγοι Ἑλλήνων. τίς γὰρ ἡ ἀποκλήρωσις, κυριολεκτεῖσθαι μὲν τὸν Δία οὐχὶ δὲ καὶ τὸν πατέρα μὲν αὐτοῦ εἶναι Κρόνον μητέρα δὲ Ῥέαν; τὸ δ᾿ ὅμοιον ποιητέον καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων ὀνομαζομένων θεῶν. τοῦτο δὲ τὸ ἔγκλημα οὐδαμῶς ἅπτεται τῶν κατά τινα ἀπόῤῥητον λόγον τὸ Σαβαὼθ τασσόντων ἐπὶ τοῦ θεοῦ ἢ τὸ Ἀδωναῒ ἤ τι τῶν λοιπῶν ὀνομάτων. ὅταν δὲ τὰ περὶ ὀνομάτων τις δύνηται τὰ ἐν ἀποῤῥήτοις φιλοσοφεῖν, πολλὰ ἂν εὕροι καὶ περὶ τῆς ἐπικλήσεως τῶν ἀγγέλων τοῦ θεοῦ· ὧν ὁ μέν τις Μιχαὴλ ἕτερος δὲ Γαβριὴλ καὶ ἄλλος Ῥαφαὴλ καλεῖται. φερωνύμως τοῖς πράγμασιν, ἃ διακονοῦνται κατὰ βούλημα τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν ὅλων ἐν τῷ παντί. τῆς δ᾿ ὁμοίας ἔχεται περὶ ὀνομάτων φιλοσοφίας καὶ ὁ ἡμέτερος Ἰησοῦς, οὗ τὸ ὄνομα μυρίους ἤδη ἐναργῶς ἑώραται δαίμονας ἐξελάσαν ψυχῶν καὶ σωμάτων, ἐνεργῆσαν εἰς ἐκείνους ἀφ᾿ ὧν ἀπηλάθησαν. ἔτι δ᾿ εἰς τὸν περὶ ὀνομάτων τόπον λεκτέον ὅτι οἱ περὶ τὴν χρῆσιν τῶν ἐπῳδῶν δεινοὶ ἱστοροῦσιν, ὅτι τὴν αὐτὴν ἐπῳδὴν εἰπόντα μὲν τῇ οἰκείᾳ διαλέκτῳ ἔστιν ἐνεργῆσαι ὅπερ ἐπαγγέλλεται ἡ ἐπῳδή· μεταλαβόντα δὲ εἰς ἄλλην οἱανδηποτοῦν φωνὴν ἔστιν ἰδεῖν ἄτονον καὶ οὐδὲν δυναμένην. οὕτως οὐ τὰ σημαινόμενα κατὰ τῶν πραγμάτων ἀλλ᾿ αἱ τῶν φωνῶν ποιότητες καὶ ἰδιότητες ἔχουσί τι δυνατὸν ἐν αὐταῖς πρὸς τάδε τινὰ ἢ τάδε. οὕτω δ᾿ ἀπολογησόμεθα διὰ τῶν τοιούτων καὶ περὶ τοῦ μέχρι θανάτου ἀγωνίζεσθαι Χριστιανοὺς, ἵνα μὴ τὸν Δία θεὸν ἀναγορεύσωσι μηδ᾿ ἄλλῃ διαλέκτῳ αὐτὸν ὀνομάσωσιν. ἢ γὰρ ἀορίστως ὁμολογοῦσι τὸ κοινὸν ὄνομα τὸ θεὸς ἢ καὶ μετὰ προσθήκης τῆς·“ ὁ δημιουργὸς τῶν ὅλων, ὁ ποιητὴς οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς, ὁ καταπέμψας τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων τούσδε τινὰς τοὺς σοφούς“· ὡς τῷ ὀνόματι ἐφαρμοζόμενον τὸ θεὸς ὄνομα δύναμίν τινα παρὰ ἀνθρώποις ἐπιτελεῖ. πολλὰ δ᾿ ἂν καὶ ἄλλα λέγοιτο εἰς τὸν περὶ ὀνομάτων τόπον πρὸς τοὺς οἰομένους δεῖν ἀδιαφορεῖν περὶ τῆς χρήσεως αὐτῶν. καὶ εἴπερ θαυμάζεται Πλάτων εἰπὼν ἐν Φιλήβῳ· „τὸ δ᾿ ἐμὸν δέος, ὦ Πρώταρχε. περὶ τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν θεῶν οὐκ ὀλίγον.“ ἐπεὶ Φίληβος θεὸν τὴν ἡδονὴν εἶπεν ὁ προσδιαλεγόμενος τῷ Σωκράτει· πῶς οὐ μᾶλλον τῆς εὐλαβείας ἀποδεξόμεθα Χριστιανοὺς, μηδὲν τῶν ἐν ταῖς μυθοποιΐαις παραλαμβανομένων ὀνομάτων προσάπτοντας τῷ τοῦ παντὸς δημιουργῷ; ἀλλὰ γὰρ τούτων ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος ἅλις.
pass_a_gloss: And perhaps the danger is not less for the one who brings down the name of God or the name of the good upon things which it is not proper to do, than for the one who exchanges names which are unspeakable and some of which are applied to lesser things and others to greater things. And I do not say that to Zeus is immediately associated the son of Cronus and Rhea and the husband of Hera and the brother of Poseidon and the father of Athena and Artemis and the one who had intercourse with his daughter Persephone, or that to Apollo is associated the son of Leto and Zeus and the brother of Artemis and the brother of Hermes, and whatever other things the wise men of Celsus' doctrines and the ancient theologians of the Greeks bring. For what is the explanation, to be spoken of literally, that Zeus is not the father of Cronus and the mother Rhea? And the same thing must be done with respect to the other named gods. But this accusation does not apply at all to those who assign the name Sabaoth to God or Adonai or any of the other names. When someone is able to philosophize about the things concerning names which are in the unspeakable things, they would find many things also concerning the invocation of the angels of God, of whom one is called Michael and another Gabriel and another Raphael. They are named according to the things which they serve, according to the will of God of all things in the universe. And our Jesus also has a similar philosophy concerning names, whose name has already been clearly seen to cast out myriads of demons from souls and bodies, having worked upon those from whom they were cast out. And yet, concerning the place of names, it must be said that those who are skilled in the use of incantations tell that, when the same incantation is spoken in its own dialect, it is able to work what it promises, but when it is translated into any other language, it is seen to be weak and unable to do anything. Thus, it is not the things signified according to the things, but the qualities and properties of the sounds that have some power in them with respect to certain things. Thus, we will apologize through such things also concerning the Christians who struggle until death, so that they may not proclaim Zeus as God nor name him in any other language. For either they confess the common name God without distinction or also with the addition of 'the creator of all things, the maker of heaven and earth, the one who sent to the race of men these certain wise men', as if the name God is applied to a certain power among men. Many other things could also be said concerning the place of names to those who think that they should be indifferent to the use of them. And if Plato is admired for saying in Philebus, 'My fear, O Protarchus, is not small concerning the names of the gods', since Philebus said that God is pleasure, the one conversing with Socrates, how much more will we accept the reverence of Christians, who do not apply any of the names taken from myths to the creator of the universe? But enough of these things for now.

pass_b_english: Perhaps the danger is no less for someone who drags the name of God — or the name of the Good — down onto things where it does not belong, than for someone who swaps around names that belong to unspeakable mysteries, attaching some to lesser realities and others to greater ones. I am not claiming that the moment you say "Zeus" you immediately conjure the son of Cronus and Rhea, the husband of Hera, the brother of Poseidon, the father of Athena and Artemis, and the one who coupled with his own daughter Persephone; or that "Apollo" instantly summons the son of Leto and Zeus, the brother of Artemis, and the half-brother of Hermes, along with whatever other genealogies the wise men of Celsus's school and the ancient Greek theologians attach to their gods. After all, what literal sense does it make to say Zeus is not the child of Cronus and Rhea? The same problem dogs every other named deity. Yet this charge does not touch those who assign to God names like Sabaoth, Adonai, or any of the other revered titles. When someone is able to reflect philosophically on names that belong to the unspeakable realm, they will discover much also about the invocation of God's angels — Michael, Gabriel, Raphael — each named in keeping with the specific service they render by the will of the God of all things throughout the universe. Our own Jesus embodies a comparable philosophy of names: his name has already been seen to cast out myriads of demons from souls and bodies, exercising power over the very persons from whom those demons were expelled. Furthermore, on the subject of names we must note that experts in incantations report a striking fact: the same incantation, spoken in its native tongue, can accomplish what it promises, but once translated into any other language it becomes feeble and utterly ineffective. Evidently, then, it is not the meanings conveyed by the words that carry the power, but the particular qualities and properties of the sounds themselves, which possess a certain efficacy toward specific ends. By such reasoning we can also defend Christians who struggle to the death rather than proclaim Zeus as God or name him in any other tongue. For they either confess the bare, common name "God" without qualification, or they add the description "the Creator of all things, the Maker of heaven and earth, the One who sent these certain wise men to the human race" — as if the very name "God" when so applied exerts a distinctive power among people. Many other things could be said on this topic to those who imagine that the use of such names is a matter of indifference. And if Plato wins admiration for saying in the Philebus, "My fear, Protarchus, is no small matter concerning the names of the gods" — spoken because Philebus had identified God with pleasure, the interlocutor of Socrates — how much more should we welcome the reverence of Christians, who refuse to attach any name drawn from mythology to the Creator of the universe? But enough on these matters for now.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the complex genealogical lists and the philosophical distinction between the meaning of words and the properties of sounds. The translation of 'ἀπόῤῥητον' as 'unspeakable' and 'ἐπῳδῶν' as 'incantations' is appropriate for the context of the argument. The Plato reference is correctly identified as the dialogue Philebus. All clauses in the Greek are accounted for in both Pass A and Pass B.
